newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Road to Sri Lanka's Mannar a desolate journey.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Road to Sri Lanka's Mannar a desolate journey.

text.p: For the first time in years, buses carrying civilians are passing through the remote northwestern Sri Lankan village of Murunkan in the former heartland of Tamil Tiger rebels.
Once a bustling trading centre, there is little to see in dusty and desolate Murunkan but stray mules and a few heavily armed Sri Lankan soldiers.
The bleakness of Murunkan can be seen along the 100-km (60-mile) highway from Vavuniya in the northeast to Mannar in the northwest.

Captured by Sri Lankan armed forces in late February from Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, it is a stretch of road enjoying an uneasy peace but still deeply scarred by the country's ethnic war.
VILLAGE RUINS SHOW MARKS OF VIBRANT PAST

At the foot of the Giants Tank, a reservoir that feeds the surrounding region's 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) of rice fields, the village still bears signs of its vibrant past, when farmers came in large numbers to trade in rice, cattle and fish.
But today, Murunkan's roofless trading houses are in a shambles, the train station leveled and storefronts pocked with bullet holes.
"For the first time since 1988, the road is now open to public traffic," said Colonel Udaya Ariyaratne, commander of the forces in Mannar, about 24 km (15 miles) west of Murunkan.
"We are well fortified along the entire route and we don't plan on allowing the LTTE to take control of it ever again," Ariyaratne told Reuters during a recent visit to Mannar.

The LTTE, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, put up little resistance as troops advanced to take the road in a massive offensive launched in February. The war is now in its 14th year.
ARMY SAYS TAMIL TIGERS BLEW UP BRIDGES
"Much of the damage seen around was not caused by our offensive," said a sergeant-major in charge of a small army camp at Paraiyanalankulam, about half-way between Vavuniya and Mannar.
"The LTTE blew up bridges and culverts as they withdrew, but the buildings and all that are the results of prolonged war," he said, pointing to destroyed houses.
The LTTE were not immediately available for comment.
The rebels still control vast stretches of land to the south and to the north of the road. But the military believes they have less capability of attacking the road from the south.

"Just 500 metres (550 yards) to the north of the road, they are there. It is possible for them to attack the road's defences from the north. But we have systems in place to prevent them," the sergeant-major said.

The opening of the road is seen as a boon to the battered economy of Mannar, a once thriving fishing town 240 km (150 miles) north of the capital Colombo. Until the road opened, Mannar was connected to the rest of the country only by sea.
OPENING OF ROAD BRINGS HOPE

"Now, with the road open, we are optimistic of selling our fish harvest and rice harvest to other regions and bringing some money into people's hands," said Velupillai Vishvalingam, a deputy government administrator of Mannar.
Four buses a day traverse the pot-holed road, reduced to nothing more than a dirt track in some places, taking civilians between Mannar and Vavuniya.
While fish and rice are sent out of Mannar, trucks bring in flour, soft drinks, cement and other commodities until recently considered luxuries by the town's population of about 30,000.
But supplies, including medicine, are limited by the military, fearing some may fall into the hands of rebels, who still dominate areas just north of Mannar.
And life for the few people living along the road is far from settled. The majority moved off the road along with rebels as they withdrew ahead of advancing troops.

"Our fields are on the other side (of the road). The children's schools are on the other side. But we can't cross the road to get to any of them," said Velupulle Sellamma, a mother of five from Ganeshapuram, a village of 27 families along the roadside.
Two of her children decided to go with the rebels as they withdrew and are now living among some 17,000 refugees at Madhu, a village to the north of the road which is under LTTE control.
"We're afraid of attacks by the LTTE for not having gone with them over to their side," said Sellamma's husband, P. Velupulle.
"They have been dislodged from their homes and fields and are living as refugees," said Xavier Cruez, a Catholic priest in Mannar. "Now we have to consider the plight of these people too."
